title: The first-time host guide: running your first one to three short-term rentals
summary: An operations checklist for new hosts: permits, setup, listing, five guest messages, cleaning, pricing basics and earning your first reviews.
body_markdown:
[All posts](https://prohost.ai/blog)


**Your first one to three short-term rentals are where you set the habits the rest of your hosting runs on. The listing, the five guest messages, the turnover, the price and the first reviews: get those right in the first month and everything after is repetition. This guide is the operations checklist for a new host, in the order you'll need it, with the rules from Airbnb's own help pages and free templates you can copy.**


## Key takeaways


- **Check the rules before the listing.** City and county permits and occupancy taxes decide whether you can host at all. Do this first.
- **Five messages cover a stay:** pre-booking, booking confirmation, check-in, checkout and a review request. Schedule them once.
- **Your cleaner is your product.** Write the turnover checklist before the first booking, require photos, and line up a backup.
- **Price on total cost.** Airbnb compares your total price, fees included, with similar nearby listings ([Airbnb](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/39) ).
- **Your first reviews matter most.** A rating shows only after three reviews, and Airbnb designs search so new listings show up well. Treat your first ten stays as the most important ones.
- **Answer new inquiries and reservation requests within 24 hours.** That window is how Airbnb measures your response rate, which counts toward Superhost status and search placement ([Airbnb](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/430) ).

## Where we're coming from


We host in Hawaii, the Smokies and Joshua Tree, and we've earned a[4.99 rating across thousands of guest stays](https://prohost.ai/about) . Before ProhostAI I spent 6 years at Airbnb as a staff data scientist on the hosting team. The lesson that applies most to a first-time host: the hosts who do well early aren't the ones with the best property. They're the ones who answer fast, describe the place accurately, and never cancel.


## Step 1: rules, permits and taxes (week 0)


Before you write a word of the listing:


- **Zoning and permits.** Many cities and counties require a short-term rental permit, and some don't allow stays under 30 days in residential zones. Search your city and county name with "short-term rental permit."
- **Occupancy taxes.** Airbnb collects occupancy tax in many places, but not everywhere. Check Airbnb's list of[where it collects and remits](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2509) . In Hawaii, for example, it collects nothing and you file yourself.
- **Insurance.** Your homeowner's policy may not cover paid guests. Ask your insurer. Airbnb's AirCover for hosts includes up to $3 million in damage protection and $1 million in liability insurance, and Airbnb notes the damage protection is "not an insurance policy" ([AirCover](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/3733) ).
- **HOA or lease.** Read it for a rental ban.


We've written market guides for the places we host:[Hawaii](https://prohost.ai/blog/hawaii-short-term-rental-guide) (and[Hawaii taxes](https://prohost.ai/blog/hawaii-short-term-rental-taxes-and-county-rules) ),[the Smokies](https://prohost.ai/blog/smoky-mountains-cabin-rental-guide) and[Joshua Tree](https://prohost.ai/blog/joshua-tree-short-term-rental-guide) .


## Step 2: set up the property (week 1)


```text
FIRST-UNIT SETUP CHECKLIST


Access
[ ] Smart lock or keypad (a code per guest beats a lockbox)
[ ] Backup way in (spare code, lockbox with key, neighbor)


Safety
[ ] Smoke and CO alarms on every level, tested
[ ] Fire extinguisher in the kitchen; first-aid kit
[ ] Emergency info posted: address, nearest hospital, your number


Sleep and bath (2 full sets per bed minimum)
[ ] Linens, pillows, mattress protectors
[ ] Towels: bath, hand, wash, plus 1 extra per guest
[ ] Blackout curtains in bedrooms


Kitchen
[ ] Coffee maker + coffee, kettle, basic spices, oil, salt and pepper
[ ] Pots, pans, knives that cut, cutting board, dish soap, sponges


Supplies (stock for 2 turnovers)
[ ] Toilet paper, paper towels, trash bags, hand soap
[ ] Shampoo, conditioner, body wash


Connectivity
[ ] Wi-Fi tested in every room; network name and password on a card
[ ] TV with streaming apps signed in (or signed out each turnover)


Owner's closet (locked)
[ ] Spare linens, supplies, light bulbs, batteries, filters


```


## Step 3: write the listing (week 1)


Airbnb's search article says better ratings and reviews, more saves and bookings, price, location, listing details and photos all play a part, and that "high-quality listing photos and videos help attract guests' attention" ([Airbnb](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/39) ). For a new listing:


- **Photos:** hire a photographer if you can. Shoot in daylight, every room, the view and the bathroom.
- **Title and description:** say what's true and specific. "Two-bedroom cabin with hot tub, 10 minutes to the park entrance" beats adjectives.
- **Accuracy over flattery.** Accuracy is one of the six review categories. A listing that oversells gets a lower accuracy score.
- **House rules:** short, about what would cause a cancellation (pets, parties, parking, quiet hours).
- **Instant Book:** Airbnb says listings that can be booked instantly "may rank higher" ([article 39](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/39) ). Turn it on with house rules that screen for what matters to you.


## Step 4: schedule the five messages (week 1)


Five messages cover a stay. Write them once, schedule them, and stop typing them by hand. We have[full templates on the blog](https://prohost.ai/blog/airbnb-message-templates) . The short version:


1. **Pre-booking** (Instant Book): two or three facts that would cause a cancellation, one question.
2. **Booking confirmation:** thanks, dates, what happens next. No door code.
3. **Check-in instructions:** the day before, with address, parking, door code and Wi-Fi.
4. **Checkout instructions:** the evening before. Three steps at most.
5. **Review request:** the day after checkout. Ask for a review, never a rating.


## Step 5: set up the turnover (week 2)


The cleaner sees the property more than you do. Set them up to succeed:


- **A written checklist** room by room, with what "done" looks like.
- **Photos at the end of every clean:** kitchen, bathrooms, beds, anything that breaks often.
- **A supply list** they restock from, and a way to tell you when it's low.
- **A backup cleaner** before you need one.
- **Pay on time,** every time. A cleaner who's paid late finds other hosts.


If you need help finding cleaners or a handyman, the[ProhostAI vendor directory](https://prohost.ai/vendors) lists local service providers by city.


## Step 6: price it (week 2)


- **Start a little below comparable listings** for your first few stays. Airbnb's search says listings "priced below other comparable listings in the area" tend to rank higher, comparing total price ([article 39](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/39) ).
- **Watch the cleaning fee.** It's part of the total price the guest compares.
- **Know Airbnb's fee.** Most hosts pay a single 15.5% host-only service fee since 2026 ([Airbnb](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1857) ). Set your price knowing that comes out of it.
- **Do the math.** Use our free[Airbnb profit calculator](https://prohost.ai/tools/airbnb-profit-calculator) and[ROI calculator](https://prohost.ai/tools/roi-calculator) to see what you keep after fees, cleaning and costs.
- **Add dynamic pricing once you're booking.** A tool like[PriceLabs](https://prohost.ai/integrations/pricelabs) adjusts rates daily from market demand.


## Step 7: earn the first reviews (weeks 3 to 8)


- **A rating appears after three reviews** ([Airbnb](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/13) ). Until then, guests see "new."
- **Both sides have 14 days** after checkout to review, and reviews post when both are in or the window closes.
- **Write your guest's review promptly.** Reviews post when both sides have submitted, so yours shouldn't be the one holding it up.
- **Fix what the first guests mention,** before the next guest arrives.
- **Answer fast.** Response rate is "the percentage of new inquiries and reservation requests you responded to within 24 hours" over 30 days, and it affects Superhost status and search placement ([article 430](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/430) ).
- **Never cancel.** Host cancellations carry fees from 10% to 50% of the unstayed nights and can block your calendar ([article 990](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/990) ).


More in our guide to[getting more 5-star reviews](https://prohost.ai/blog/how-to-get-more-5-star-reviews) .


## Going from one unit to three


When you add a second and third unit, three things change:


- **Templates become per-listing.** Parking and checkout differ. Use placeholders and per-listing versions.
- **Cleanings overlap.** Two checkouts on one Saturday need two cleaners or a plan.
- **Messages double.** This is the point where most hosts start using software for replies, not just schedules.

## FAQ


**How much does it cost to start hosting?** It depends on the property. Furnishing and supplies are one-time costs; cleaning, supplies, utilities, platform fees and software are ongoing. Use the[profit calculator](https://prohost.ai/tools/airbnb-profit-calculator) for your numbers.


**Do I need software for one listing?** Not on day one. Airbnb's scheduled messages and quick replies cover a single listing. Software pays off when you have more than one channel, more than one unit, or messages you can't answer in time.


**How fast do I need to reply?** Within 24 hours for new inquiries and requests to protect your response rate. Faster is better for bookings.


**When will I get my first review?** After your first guest checks out and reviews, within 14 days. Your rating shows after three.


**Should I turn on Instant Book?** Airbnb says instantly bookable listings may rank higher. Most new hosts benefit from it, with clear house rules.


## The takeaway


Check the rules, set up the property, write an accurate listing, schedule five messages, give your cleaner a checklist, price on total cost and protect your first reviews. That's the whole operation for your first units. Do it once, carefully, and the next unit is a copy. For more, see the rest of[the blog](https://prohost.ai/blog) .
